questions.q: What does a Deployment give you that a bare Pod does not?
o: Replacement of failed pods, rolling updates and rollbacks
A permanent IP address that never changes for the pod
Direct access to the node's physical disks
Automatic encryption of all traffic between pods
questions.w: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets that keep the desired number of pods running. A bare pod is not recreated if its node fails.

questions.q: Why do clients call a Service instead of a pod IP?
o: Pod IPs change on replacement, while the Service has a stable name and IP
Pods cannot receive requests directly from other pods
A Service makes each pod run faster than before
Pod IPs are only valid inside the same node
questions.w: The Service load-balances across ready pods that match its label selector and has a DNS name such as `payments.bank.svc.cluster.local`.

questions.q: Which probe failure removes a pod from the Service without restarting it?
o: Readiness
Liveness
Startup
Rollout
questions.w: A failing liveness probe restarts the container. A failing readiness probe only stops traffic until it passes again.

questions.q: A database outage restarts every pod of a service. What is the probable mistake?
o: The liveness probe checks the database instead of only the app itself
The readiness probe is missing from the pod specification
The Service has too many replicas behind it
The image tag was set to a fixed version number
questions.w: Keep dependency checks in readiness. Liveness should answer only whether this process is stuck.

questions.q: A JVM takes 45 seconds to start and the liveness probe starts failing at 30 seconds, killing the pod repeatedly. What is the best fix?
o: Add a startup probe that allows enough time before liveness begins
Remove all probes so Kubernetes stops checking the pod
Lower the memory limit so the JVM starts quicker
Give the pod more replicas so some can finish starting
questions.w: A startup probe holds back liveness and readiness until it succeeds, protecting slow starts without loosening liveness.

questions.q: What happens when a container exceeds its memory limit and when it exceeds its CPU limit?
o: Memory: it is OOMKilled. CPU: it is throttled
Memory: it is throttled. CPU: it is OOMKilled
Both: the pod is moved to a larger node
Both: the limit is ignored until the next deployment
questions.w: CPU is compressible, so the container only gets slower. Memory is not, so the kernel kills the process (exit code 137).

questions.q: A rolling update has `maxUnavailable: 0` and `maxSurge: 1`. What does that mean?
o: A new pod starts first and must be ready before an old one is stopped
Old pods are stopped first and new ones start afterwards
All pods are replaced at the same instant for speed
Only one pod is ever allowed to be running at a time
questions.w: Capacity never drops, provided readiness probes are correct and the app shuts down gracefully.

questions.q: What is true about a Kubernetes Secret by default?
o: It is only base64-encoded, so access must be restricted with RBAC
It is encrypted with a key that only the pod can read
It is hashed so the original value can never be recovered
It is stored outside the cluster in a separate vault
questions.w: Enable encryption at rest for etcd, limit who can read Secrets, and prefer an external secret manager for sensitive credentials.
